Q-CHANG / SERVICE DESIGN / 2022

Change Date

One date changes. Everyone has to move.

Making room for customer changes across technician schedules, service teams, and promotion planning.

Explore the case ↓

My contribution

Research analysis, workflow mapping & presentation

Home services · Bangkok · COVID-era research

I analyzed rescheduling data and presented problems and possible directions. My manager decided how to proceed; the operational changes were carried out by the relevant teams.

My process01The signal02Behind the date03A five-day window04What changed05My reflection

MY PROCESS

From records to a problem the team could act on.

Eight steps from examining rescheduling requests to proposing a direction.

  1. 01

    The problem

    Approximately 4,000 service rescheduling records.

  2. 02

    Classify the reasons

    Unforeseen circumstances, system issues, and behavior.

  3. 03

    Choose the data

    Focus on our website and partner platforms, grouped by sales channel.

  4. 04

    Look for patterns

    Examine recurring patterns in booking dates and date changes.

  5. 05

    Identify a signal

    Notice booking dates that coincided with promotions, and investigate further.

  6. 06

    Present the findings

    Summarize the patterns and questions for my manager.

  7. 07

    Interview people

    Speak with internal staff and customers to understand the context behind the records.

  8. 08

    Frame the problem

    Define the problem and propose directions for the team to decide how to proceed.

Approximately 4,000 refers to 3,999 records. The promotion pattern was a signal to investigate, not proof of causation.

01 / The signal

Almost 9 in 10 changes went through staff.

A three-month sample showed how much of the rescheduling journey passed through people. That became the starting point for examining the coordination behind each request.

3,999rescheduling records

Source data: March–May 2022

Handled by staff
3,545 ≈ 89%
Customer self-service
454 ≈ 11%

3,999 records in total. Presented to executives as approximately 4,000 for recall. Records are not unique customers; these figures describe the sample, not an improvement rate.

02 / Behind the date

A new date could set off a chain of work.

If the original technician was unavailable, the request could move through several people before the customer had another workable appointment.

  1. 01

    Customer

    Requests a new date

  2. 02

    CS · Customer service

    Checks the request

  3. 03

    Technician

    Confirms availability

  4. 04

    IS · Coordination

    Looks for a replacement

  5. 05

    Customer

    Reconfirms the appointment

If no team was available: further coordination, another date, or refund handling. This is a simplified account of the existing process, not a new automated workflow.

THE DESIGN QUESTION

How could the service accommodate change before turning to fees?

I brought the discussion back to preparation: available technicians, clear expectations, and enough time to coordinate. The final decision on cancellation or change fees is not documented here.

03 / A five-day window

Give people time to act on a reminder.

Our working assumption was that a next-day service reminder prompted some customers to remember the booking—and call to change it at the last minute.

Working assumption · not a proven causal result

  1. 5 days before

    Proposed earlier reminder

    Time to review the appointment and coordinate a change.

  2. 1 day before

    Previous reminder timing

    A possible trigger for last-minute requests.

  3. Service day

    Scheduled visit

    Customer and technician need a shared plan.

Five days was a coordination compromise for customers, technicians, and the platform. It was not an experimentally proven optimum or a measure of how far customers moved their dates. The production rollout of this reminder is not confirmed here.

04 / What changed

The response reached beyond the calendar UI.

These are team actions I recall following the work. My contribution was analysis and presentation; my manager determined the implementation approach.

01

CS + IS

A shared way to explain changes

The teams developed response scripts to explain rescheduling and its effects to customers and technicians.

02

TECHNICIAN OPERATIONS

Clearer calendar discipline

Rules for opening and closing technician calendars became stricter.

03

MARKETING + FIELD CONSULTANTS

Prepare capacity before promotions

Marketing and field consultants coordinated campaign dates and technician readiness. Marketing used LINE groups to remind technicians to update calendars.

04

TECHNICIAN ONBOARDING

Explain availability from the start

Onboarding content was expanded to explain how technicians should open and close their calendars.

＋

A small customer-facing addition

I also worked on an add-to-calendar UI to help customers remember appointments. Its release status and usage were not recorded in the evidence available for this case.

QUALITATIVE OBSERVATION

I recall fewer date changes after calendar rules became stricter. There is no before-and-after measurement here, and the effect cannot be attributed to one change alone.

05 / My reflection

A feature request opened a wider service conversation.

The value of my work was making the coordination problem visible enough for others to act on. I learned to connect customer requests with operational constraints, and to make clear where my recommendations ended and team decisions began.
